Package com.irurueta.authserver.serviceclient.device

Class DeviceFlowCli

java.lang.Object
com.irurueta.authserver.serviceclient.device.DeviceFlowCli
All Implemented Interfaces:
org.springframework.boot.CommandLineRunner
@Component @Profile("device-flow") public class DeviceFlowCli extends Object implements org.springframework.boot.CommandLineRunner
Command-line client of the OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant (RFC 8628): requests a device code, prints the user code and the verification URI, then polls the token endpoint honouring interval, slow_down, authorization_pending and expired_token.

Running it from the packaged jar: the class is a runner of the device-flow Spring profile, so 

 java -jar service-client-boot.jar --spring.profiles.active=device-flow --device-flow.issuer=http://localhost:9000
runs it instead of the regular application (which is unaffected without the profile). Optional settings are --device-flow.client-id, --device-flow.scope and --device-flow.print-access-token=true.

Output, one line each and in this order, so a test can parse them: 

 User code: ABCD-EFGH
 Verification URI: http://localhost:9000/oauth2/device_verification
 Verification URI (complete): http://localhost:9000/oauth2/device_verification?user_code=ABCD-EFGH
 Device flow completed: token_type=Bearer expires_in=300 scope=profile documents.read refresh_token=false
The tokens themselves are never printed unless print-access-token is set, which adds an Access token: ... line. On any failure the process ends with a non-zero exit code.

Why it lives in src/main: the end-to-end test runs the packaged service-client jar, so the CLI has to be in it; it is a genuine, reusable tool of the application and not a test double.
